title: Get to Know May : Mike Diaz, Senior Autonomy Release Engineer
summary: May creates the autonomous driving system that lets ride-hail vehicles reason through the road in real time. Built for safer streets, smoother rides and…
body_markdown:
## What is your title and what do you do at May Mobility?


I am a Senior Autonomy Release Engineer. The Release Team scopes, manages, tracks, and vets the software that goes onto May’s vehicles from pre-release to deployment in the field to end of use. The resulting bundle includes the autonomy stack as well as rider experience software, other module firmware, etc. We ensure that prior to release, stakeholders are informed on the incoming software content, the value it brings, and provide views into the data to back up those claims.


## What was the 'aha!' moment that made you realize autonomous vehicles were the future you wanted to work on?


I had been working for a few years in automotive engineering in the area of production hybrid and electric vehicle powertrain software and controls. At the time, it was the ‘big thing’ hitting the automotive space. I enjoyed being at the technological forefront of the industry, and by 2015 it was clear the next big thing was autonomous driving, and it was coming fast.


As hybrid and electric vehicles became mainstream, the technical challenges in getting their software and controls production-ready waned and I was interested in jumping into autonomous technology as there was clearly rising momentum in the industry.


I noticed that autonomous vehicles looked good and were capable of impressive demos (and big VC funding followed suit), but I could tell there was a lot left between that research-level stuff and bringing AVs to public roads with real consumers riding them and at scale. That was when I truly realized that I wanted to get involved and help take the raw tech to the finish line of mass acceptance and deployment.


## Why is your role important within the AV industry?


Release and deployment of AV software have to facilitate fast deployment of software iterations while keeping safety paramount. We also must keep in mind the nuances from multiple different geographical sites where we’ve deployed and the multiple generations of hardware spread throughout. While the entire company shares a common goal, some priorities are pushing development in different directions. So balancing deployment velocity with safety rigor requires constant, intentional effort. This role is pivotal in sorting through those competing forces and aims to use data in innovative ways as the prevailing constitution that guides decisions objectively and intelligently.


## What achievement at May Mobility are you most proud of?


The evolution of the company’s software release process from an early-stage, fast-moving startup approach to one based on organized cadence and criteria that still support the fast iterations that enable startups to be disruptive. It’s a fine line between a disciplined, socially responsible software release strategy and an overbearing process that stifles growth. I’m proud to have supported getting the company out of its nascent past approach and into the stage where we’re actively finding the right balance of speed and rigor - all while keeping the company operational across multiple sites and countries.


## What is something you’re working on right now that excites you?


Deployment of safety-critical products powered by software that leverages AI and is being iterated faster than ever. That used to be a 5-year cycle (think traditional automotive) or restricted to secure spaces (think power plants or airplanes). There are starting points and emerging standards as we actively develop best practices and solutions. We’re helping define what that looks like every single day. Exciting is not a big enough word to describe the feeling!


## What’s something a new hire would quickly learn about May Mobility’s culture that you can’t find on the website?


May was built on a culture of respect and socially responsible values, and that culture and value system became ingrained into every team and process at May. It guided how the company operates and how folks treat one another from the top down. This is something that is hard to get a true feel for from a website or interview until you land and really see the culture at work.


## Which of May's[core values](https://maymobility.com/meet-may/) resonates with you the most and why?


Do What's Right. In my experience, the biggest hurdle a company faces is honest communication. Less-than-honest communication internally covers up the real problems and delays real solutions. Less-than-honest communication breeds distrust and cynicism from customers and the general public. This single core value can guide us away from so many resource-wasting endeavors internally and towards achieving the goal of a dedicated customer base that really trusts that what we do with our products is in their best interest.


## What’s one thing you wish more people understood about the AV industry?


That the people have the collective power to influence the industry’s future. That may sound contrary to our interests, but it’s really not. People can and should feel empowered to demand that a technology or product provide them value. This power is central not only to a fair market but also to our way of life - especially in the United States. AVs, like any product, high-tech or not, should bring value to the customer and should guide AV deployment based on the value proposition for the customer.


Why this is not contrary to our interests as an AV company is because our ability to win depends on meeting critically unmet needs of customers that the other companies ignore out of convenience or disconnection from the people they serve.


## How do you hope to see AVs change the world?


The obvious response is the hope that AVs improve road safety by reducing fatalities and major injuries, but there’s so much more. AVs will be the first safety-critical public-facing technology to achieve widespread adoption, which means our products and industry represent a monumental shift from how things have been done in the past. In that way, we are writing the playbook for future products and industries to also bring groundbreaking technology to customers - safely, ethically, and efficiently.


## What’s a piece of advice you’d give to someone who wants to break into the AV industry?


Find the part of the AV space where your personal passion lives. Does product safety get you on your feet? Maybe it’s energy efficiency. Or perhaps it’s beautiful packaging of hardware. Maybe you’re curious about big-picture city planning for the future. The industry is so nascent and its fruits yet to be realized. There is space, and need, for big ideas in every facet. Not only with the technology itself but the future world that it will benefit! The future needs your help - find out what part calls to you and apply yourself.
